title: Talking About Mental Health More, Young Indians Not Seeking Help More
excerpt: At India Today's HealthWealth Summit, Dr Samir Parikh said three-quarters of people with difficulties still do not seek help — and feeds are not a census.
body:
• Dr Samir Parikh told India Today's HealthWealth Summit that three-quarters of people with mental health difficulties still do not seek help, and the share reaching professionals has not risen dramatically in 25 to 30 years.
  • India's National Mental Health Survey, conducted by NIMHANS, found 7.3 out of every 100 adolescents aged 13 to 17 in 12 states had a mental health disorder.
  • Worldwide, 15 out of every 100 adolescents experience a mental disorder and most do not seek help or receive care, according to the World Health Organization.
  • Reader utility: in India, free and confidential support is available around the clock through Tele-MANAS on 14416, which has handled 47,75,644 calls since October 2022.

Social media has made mental health a more visible part of public conversation in India, but visibility is not the same as treatment. That was the central warning from psychiatrists speaking at India Today's HealthWealth Summit in a session titled 'All is Hell?', where experts described a persistent gap between growing awareness and actual help-seeking, driven by stigma, limited access and gaps in mental health education.

Dr Samir Parikh, chairperson and director of the Department of Mental Health and Behavioral Sciences at Fortis Healthcare, said the perception that more people are seeking help simply because they talk about mental health more often is not entirely accurate. The proportion of people approaching mental health professionals, he said, had not risen dramatically over the past 25 to 30 years.

"Even today, three-quarters of people experiencing mental health difficulties do not seek help."

Dr Manushree Gupta, president of the Delhi Psychiatric Society, and Dr Sandeep Vohra, a psychiatrist and digital mental health entrepreneur, joined Parikh in the discussion.

Algorithms Are Not a Census

Parikh cautioned against treating social media feeds as a reflection of society at large. Once a user engages with posts about depression or anxiety, algorithms show more of the same content, creating the impression that everyone is discussing these conditions or seeking help.

"We have started mistaking the noise within our own ecosystem for reality."

The distinction matters for policy and for families. A feed crowded with mental health posts can coexist with clinics that remain out of reach, schools without counsellors and young people who still fear being judged for asking for help.

What the Numbers Show in India

The survey evidence points to a substantial, measurable burden among teenagers. Data presented to the Lok Sabha by Minister of State for Health and Family Welfare Prataprao Jadhav, based on the National Mental Health Survey carried out by the National Institute of Mental Health and Neurosciences (NIMHANS) in Bengaluru, put the figure at 7.3 out of every 100 adolescents aged 13 to 17 across 12 states with a mental health disorder.

The global picture is similar in scale. The World Health Organization says 8 out of every 100 children and 15 out of every 100 adolescents worldwide experience a mental disorder, but the majority do not seek help or receive care. Half of mental health conditions start by age 18, the WHO notes, and suicide is the third leading cause of death among people aged 15 to 29. Unaddressed conditions in adolescence, it warns, extend into adulthood and limit opportunities for leading fulfilling lives.

A Helpline That Young and Working-Age Callers Use

One service that is being used at scale is Tele-MANAS, the national tele-mental health programme launched on 10 October 2022. According to the Press Information Bureau, the programme's toll-free helpline 14416 had received 47,75,644 calls as of October 2026, through 53 cells across all 36 states and union territories, offering free, confidential, round-the-clock counselling in multiple languages.

People aged 18 to 45 accounted for 73.2 percent of 13,35,275 recorded caller profiles, and women accounted for 43.78 percent of those profiles. Callers reported emotional distress and stress linked to examinations, workplaces and relationships, as well as anxiety and sleep disturbances — the same pressures the summit panel linked to delayed help-seeking.

For diaspora families watching relatives in India, the practical test of the summit's message is simple: a conversation about mental health is a start, not a substitute for care. Tele-MANAS on 14416 requires no appointment and no travel, and counsellors can refer callers onward to specialists and local services where needed.
